The UK experienced its hottest ever summer this year, with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30C.
The Met Office has warned that extreme summer temperatures are now the new normal, while the Government’s climate advisers have predicted that British summers could be 1.6 degrees warmer and 13pc drier by 2050.
The changing climate has created trouble for gardeners, with the Royal Horticultural Society reporting a surge in people seeking advice about plants damaged by heat and drought.
Mr Roper said the rising mercury had led to plant sales tumbling by 25pc during the heatwaves because of lower demand from customers, while plant margins also fell as many products withered on the shelves.
Like-for-like sales at Blue Diamond rose by just 1.6pc during the first half of the year, though this was above the industry average.
Mr Roper said it had been the most challenging summer of his three decades in the business, adding that soaring temperatures had been compounded by hosepipe bans.
Despite the slump in plant sales, Blue Diamond was boosted by higher demand for garden furniture over the summer, with bosses pointing to the growing popularity of pergolas and garden rooms.
Restaurant sales jumped 17.7pc as demand for food and drink held up during the heatwaves.
In a further boost, Blue Diamond in June signed a three-year retail partnership with Jeremy Clarkson’s Diddly Squat farm shop to develop a range of co-branded gardening products.
Overall sales rose 12.5pc to £216m in the six months to the end of June, while pre-tax profits climbed 16pc to £24m.
Bosses said that despite subdued trading in recent weeks, the company remained well-positioned for the crucial Christmas period.
Blue Diamond, which was founded more than a century ago, has grown into the UK’s largest garden-centre operator through a string of acquisitions and new site openings.
The group has acquired three garden centres so far this year, as well as a major new warehouse on the former RAF Snaith site just off the M62.

“When the rains stopped, and the crops failed, the real problems began,” an elderly man in Boro village told us. “That’s how conflict starts, when people can no longer survive and compete for the little that is there.”
The village of Boro sits on the edge of the Okavango Delta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and climate-sensitive wetland in northwestern Botswana. The Boro River, once a dependable source of water for livestock and tourism, has been largely dry for five years, while unpredictable rainfall and prolonged drought have contributed to water shortages, crop failures, and declining grazing. Climate change, therefore, is making droughts like the one declared in 2024 more frequent and severe.
These changes reflect the growing climate pressures facing Botswana, where increasingly variable rainfall and prolonged dry periods threaten livelihoods and access to natural resources. Our study, published in September 2026 in Conflict, Security & Development, based on fieldwork conducted between July and September 2023, examined how climate change reshapes local peace and conflict dynamics and how communities like Boro actively respond to these shifts through formal and informal peacebuilding practices. The study drew on interviews and focus group discussions with 63 respondents in Boro and Maun, including farmers and herders, young people, traditional leaders, and government officials. It found that climate pressures had not tipped into violence and that the peace was maintained largely by the community’s own efforts rather than by state-led interventions.
The study also highlighted that disputes were not simply about diminishing resources. They were also shaped by longstanding grievances over land, conservation, and who gets to decide. Although based on a single village, the findings point to dynamics likely to be relevant to other climate-affected communities in southern Africa. Three lessons emerge: climate stress exposes and deepens existing grievances; local agency plays a central role in containing tensions; and weak formal institutions limit what communities can achieve on their own.
- Climate Stress Exposes Existing Grievances
In Boro, competition over resources has brought disagreements about access and ownership into sharper focus. A privately drilled borehole, for example, became the subject of a dispute over who had the right to use its water. “Some say it’s private, others say we all need water,” an elderly woman told us. “It is tearing the community apart.”
The community also described tensions over grazing and restrictions on access to wildlife areas, where some had resorted to cutting vegetation illegally to keep their livestock alive during severe droughts. A young man complained that herders from drier villages arrive in the dry season and compete with locals for pasture and tourism jobs. Climate change, then, does not cause conflict on its own. It magnifies pressures whose outcome is shaped by governance. Where people feel excluded from decisions or regard access rules as unjust, climate stress deepens existing grievances and erodes trust.
- Local Agency Keeps the Peace
Despite these tensions, residents described ways of resolving disputes before they escalated into violence. Traditional leaders, including the chief and ward headmen, intervened in disagreements over water, land and encroachment. “When people started fighting over water and land, the chief and elders stepped in,” an elderly man recalled. “They listened to everyone and helped us find common ground. Without them, things could have gotten worse.”
Households have also adapted to changing conditions. Some elderly women reported planting crops that mature more quickly and require less rainfall, while others diversified their livelihoods by harvesting thatching grass and making handicrafts. “Even with small fields, we can still get something to eat and avoid quarrels with neighbours over land,” one woman said.
These responses show that peacebuilding is not confined to mediating disputes. It also involves protecting livelihoods, adapting to environmental pressures and finding practical ways to reduce competition. In Boro, these efforts depend on trusted local leaders, the willingness of community members to negotiate, and everyday acts of restraint.
- Weak Structures Leave Communities Carrying the Load
However, local efforts have limits. Traditional leaders can mediate a dispute, but they cannot change national land-use rules, open restricted wildlife areas to grazing or pay for crops destroyed by elephants. Those powers sit with the Tawana Land Board and the Department of Wildlife and National Parks, which communities described as distant and slow to respond. “Decisions about our land are made without involving us,” an elderly resident said. “It makes us feel ignored and excluded.”
Officials we interviewed acknowledged that water and forage shortages were pushing wildlife closer to the village. Where losses went uncompensated, some villagers organised night patrols to chase elephants away, at times putting them at odds with conservation laws. When formal institutions are weak, frustration with the state can become a source of tension in its own right. Climate adaptation must therefore strengthen these structures and make them answerable to the communities they serve. Measures that improve water access or support livelihoods will be difficult to sustain if they leave unresolved disagreements about who can use resources, under what conditions and with whose consent.
Community representatives, traditional leaders, land and conservation authorities, and community trusts could work together to agree on clear rules for resource access during drought, covering seasonal grazing, water use, and compensation for wildlife losses. Giving chiefs existing peacemaking roles a formal footing, through local climate-peace committees, would build on what already works. Young people and elders should take part together.
What Boro teaches us
The experience of Boro offers a lesson for communities facing similar pressures: climate change can intensify competition, but the path from scarcity to conflict is shaped by social relationships and the governance of natural resources. As climate change intensifies, Boro’s residents have shown that communities can keep the peace under severe climate stress. Their efforts, however, cannot resolve the structural problems that restrict access to resources and exclude communities from decisions.
Supporting peace in a changing climate means strengthening local initiatives while making resource governance more inclusive and responsive. Communities can mediate disputes and adapt their livelihoods, but lasting peace also requires fair rules for resource access, meaningful participation in decision-making, and institutions that respond to local needs.

ByMark Elliott, Reporting fromTelford and Alex James, West Midlands
Published
A recycling plant in Telford says it handled a record number of fridges over the summer as the hot weather caused more appliances to break down.
Retailer AO, which operates the Halesfield plant, said June and August were its busiest months ever for fridge recycling.
Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office, leading to more white goods failing and needing to be scrapped.
Dave Ware, commercial director at AO, said the company was potentially having its biggest year, with between 570,000 and 580,000 fridges coming through its doors.
"What we had was... the hottest temperatures ever, and high temperatures kill fridges in a household," he said.
Ware said the length of this summer's heatwaves had made it particularly challenging, as it meant a longer peak in the number of units being recycled.
"The volume of fridges being recycled across the country was significantly higher than we've ever seen, and for a much longer period of time. The peak is usually seven to 10 days; we're talking five to six weeks," he said.
In August, dozens of councils were forced to stop collecting white goods because of a major backlog, caused by a national shortage of the specialist facilities needed to safely process the appliances.
The backlog was made worse by the closure of three of the UK's 10 full-scale processing plants in the past 14 months, while the remaining sites cannot operate in temperatures above 30C.
Ware said keeping the plant's 80-tonne crushing machine, Bertha, cool was important in order to safely remove pollutants from the appliances.
"We've got some investments coming in terms of cooling the plant more, so we don't have that downtime, and we've also invested in a little bit more storage space as a buffer if there was a problem," he said.
He added that the company had already started planning for a possible surge in fridges and freezers needing recycling next summer if it was as hot as 2026.
"We haven't started taking bets in the office yet on what that's going to be... but I'm learning about El Niño and the effects of that," Ware said.
"It's trying to predict the unpredictable, which is the British summer."

With a cyclonic storm projected to make landfall in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh, the Odisha government has activated a comprehensive micro-plan to counter potential adverse weather conditions.
Revenue and Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari announced that all 30 districts in the state are expected to experience rainfall, with heavy downpours forecasted for several pockets.
Addressing the media on the state’s preparedness, Minister Pujari emphasised that while the core landfall is expected in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha will experience significant collateral weather impacts. “Malkangiri district is projected to be the most affected,” Pujari stated, adding that senior administrative officials and cabinet ministers have already reached critical field locations to oversee relief and safety measures firsthand.
Robust Monitoring and 24/7 Control Rooms
To ensure immediate response and seamless communication, round-the-clock control rooms have been established from the district level up to the state headquarters. “Ministers and senior officers are already on the ground so they can take immediate, localised action wherever necessary,” Pujari noted.
Proactive Flood Management
Beyond immediate cyclone winds and rains, the government is keeping a close eye on potential secondary hazards, particularly river flooding. Acknowledging that rainfall in upstream Chhattisgarh directly impacts Odisha’s river systems, proactive steps are already underway. “Rainfall in Chhattisgarh means the Mahanadi River will swell. Therefore, proper water management is our top priority,” Pujari explained. He confirmed that discussions have already been held with Chhattisgarh authorities to ensure coordinated water regulation and prevent any unexpected flood situations downstream.
The state administration has urged citizens to stay alert, follow official advisories, and cooperate with local authorities as disaster response teams remain on high alert across the region.
